content: The chokecherry, scientifically known as Prunus virginiana, is a species of bird cherry (Prunus subgenus Padus) that is native to North America. It is widely distributed across the continent, except in the deep southern and far northern regions. This plant typically grows as a suckering shrub or a small tree, reaching a height of approximately 5 meters. The leaves of the chokecherry are oval-shaped, measuring between 3 and 10 centimeters in length, and have coarsely serrated edges. Its flowers bloom in racemes containing 15 to 30 individual flowers, which appear in late spring, well after the leaves have emerged. The fruit of the chokecherry is small, about 1 centimeter in diameter, and bright red in color. The fruit is known for its highly astringent and sour taste. Similar to chokeberries, chokecherries are rich in antioxidant pigment compounds, particularly anthocyanins. There are two recognized varieties of chokecherry: 1. Common Chokecherry (Prunus virginiana var. virginiana): Found in eastern North America, its leaves are either hairless underneath or have downy hairs only in the vein axils. 2. Western Chokecherry (Prunus virginiana var. demissa): Found in western North America, its leaves are distinctly downy on the underside. In the wild, chokecherry is often considered a pest because it serves as a host for tent caterpillars, which can pose a threat to other fruit plants. However, cultivated varieties of chokecherry, such as the 'Goertz' cultivar, are appreciated for their non-astringent and more palatable fruit. Research at the University of Saskatchewan is focused on developing new cultivars to enhance chokecherry production and processing. Chokecherry is closely related to the black cherry (Prunus serotina), which is native to eastern North America. It can be distinguished from black cherry by its smaller size (black cherry can grow up to 30 meters tall), smaller leaves, and red ripe fruit (as opposed to black ripe fruit). The name chokecherry has also been used to refer to the related Manchurian or Amur cherry (Prunus maackii), sometimes called Amur chokecherry. Chokecherry is toxic to horses, particularly after the leaves have wilted, such as following frost exposure or branch breakage. Wilting releases cyanide, which makes the plant sweeter and more palatable but highly dangerous. Ingesting 5 to 10 kilograms of foliage can be fatal to horses. Symptoms of poisoning in horses include heavy breathing, agitation, and weakness. The leaves of the chokecherry also serve as a food source for the caterpillars of various Lepidoptera species. For more information, refer to the list of Lepidoptera that feed on Prunus species.
